title: What the Bible Really Says About Money | Proverbs 22:7
metaDescription: A pastoral look at what Scripture teaches about money, debt, saving, and generosity from Proverbs. Money isn't what matters most - Jesus is. Watch and read.
bodyHtml:
Here is a question worth sitting with for a moment: if someone offered you three million dollars with no wisdom, or a lifetime of wisdom with no money, which would you choose? Most of us would grab the cash. But the book of Proverbs quietly insists we would be choosing wrong.

In this message closing out our Guidance for Today series through Proverbs, we tackled a topic many of us would rather avoid in church: money. It is a subject often twisted and manipulated, so we approached it carefully — not from our perspective, but from God's. And here is the surprising thing: talking honestly about money turns out to be less a financial conversation and more a deeply spiritual one.

Money Is Not What Matters Most

Proverbs opens by ranking wisdom above wealth:

"Choose my instruction instead of silver, knowledge rather than choice gold, for wisdom is more precious than rubies, and nothing you desire can compare with her." — Proverbs 8:10–11

Why is wisdom worth more than gold? Because in the New Testament, wisdom is not merely a skill you develop — it is a Person. Paul writes that in Christ "are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge" (Colossians 2:3). So when Scripture says money isn't what matters most, it is ultimately pointing us to Jesus. Consider three reasons He is better than any bank account:

  • Money can be lost; your salvation cannot. Economies crash and jobs disappear, but Paul reminds us that nothing "in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus our Lord" (Romans 8:39).
  • Money cannot buy happiness; Jesus gives lasting joy. If wealth guaranteed happiness, the richest people would be the happiest — and they plainly are not. The joy of the Lord is our strength, and it is received, not earned.
  • Money changes in value; Jesus never changes. Prices rise and dollars shrink, but "Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever" (Hebrews 13:8).

Jesus put His finger on the real issue: "For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also" (Matthew 6:21). Whatever you treasure most is what you are actually trusting as your lord. So the honest question isn't "How much money do I have?" but "What matters most to me?"

Learn to Manage Your Money Wisely

Saying money isn't ultimate doesn't mean it doesn't matter. Proverbs devotes over a hundred verses to handling money well. Here are three practical habits it commends.

Spend and save wisely

"Whoever loves pleasure will become poor; whoever loves wine and olive oil will never be rich. The wise store up choice food and olive oil, but fools gulp theirs down." — Proverbs 21:17, 20

We live in a culture of constant consumption, and technology makes overspending effortless. Two simple questions can bring restraint: Do I actually need this? and Does this fit my budget? Saving, done rightly, is not selfish — it is faithful stewardship. Building an emergency fund and living within your means honors the God who provided the income in the first place.

Understand the danger of debt

"The rich rule over the poor, and the borrower is slave to the lender." — Proverbs 22:7

Not all debt is reckless — a mortgage or responsibly used credit can be wise. But Scripture warns that debt can quietly become bondage, straining our finances, our peace, and even our relationships. If credit has become a trap for you, there is freedom in pressing pause and rebuilding healthy habits.

Give to God first

"Honor the Lord with your wealth, with the firstfruits of all your crops; then your barns will be filled to overflowing, and your vats will brim over with new wine." — Proverbs 3:9–10

Giving to God is not tipping the church for a good service — it is worship. We offer Him our first and our best, not our leftovers. And to be clear: this verse is not a magic formula that guarantees riches in exchange for offerings. That is the distortion of false teachers. Proverbs describes what normally happens, not an ironclad promise. Interestingly, the most generous people are often the most financially healthy — because when you don't worship wealth, you manage it responsibly instead of desperately.

God Wants You to Work Hard

"All hard work brings a profit, but mere talk leads only to poverty." — Proverbs 14:23

Work is not a curse invented by the enemy; it is part of God's original design, given in the garden before sin ever entered the world. Scripture calls us to avoid two extremes — the workaholic who sacrifices family, health, and faith for more money, and the person who drifts into laziness. Instead, we are invited to worship God with our work, and even to let our work become a witness. When you labor with excellence and integrity, people notice, and the door opens to point them to Christ.

The One Thing You Cannot Earn

Here is the beautiful contrast at the heart of it all: you work hard to earn money, but you cannot work to earn your salvation.

"For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, and all are justified freely by his grace through the redemption that came by Christ Jesus." — Romans 3:23–24

Every other religion says you must achieve God's favor. The gospel says you simply receive it. Jesus built the bridge we could never build — living the life we couldn't live, dying in our place, and rising again — so that we could cross to the Father freely, by faith. Christianity is not about you working your way to God; it is about God working His way to you.

A Takeaway to Carry Into the Week

Be honest before the Lord: What matters most to you — Jesus, or money? If your heart has been treasuring the wrong thing, you can turn back today. True financial freedom isn't found in having more; it is found in following the ways of God, whose ways are always better.
